pages.title: Create an account and sign in

claims.claim: An email address you can open right now. Blipmade sends the verification and password reset mail there.
claims.evidence: Register calls sendVerificationEmail (auth.ts:312) and forgot-password calls sendResetEmail (auth.ts:444); SMTP_URL is set in .env so the relay is used, but with no SMTP_URL the mailer writes the message to a file (mailer.ts:146).

claims.claim: A password of at least 8 characters. Use a password manager, because the password cannot be changed from inside a signed-in session.
claims.evidence: The minimum is 10 characters plus a lowercase, an uppercase and a digit (password.ts:57-69), and a signed-in account can change its password at POST /settings/password (settings.ts:434), covered by api/tests/settings.test.ts:127.

claims.claim: Your name is optional. You can leave it empty and set it later; the account works with the email address alone.
claims.evidence: registerSchema requires firstName and lastName with at least one character (auth.ts:53-64) and the form refuses an empty name (Register.tsx:79-80); api/tests/auth.test.ts:40 does not list an empty name as allowed.

claims.claim: Go to the register page and fill in your name, email address and password.
claims.evidence: The /register route exists (routes.tsx:106) and POST /auth/register validates name, email and password (auth.ts:286-294); api/tests/auth.test.ts:21 creates an account with a name.

claims.claim: The account is created and you are signed in straight away.
claims.evidence: Register creates the user and calls createSession in the same request (auth.ts:300-310); api/tests/auth.test.ts:21 'creates an account and signs the customer in'.

claims.claim: Blipmade sends a verification link to the address you just registered.
claims.evidence: sendVerificationEmail is called on registration (auth.ts:226, 312) and the answer states the delivery state (auth.ts:318).

claims.claim: The link opens your account and marks the address as verified.
claims.evidence: POST /auth/verify-email marks emailVerifiedAt and burns the token (auth.ts:394-417) and the VerifyEmail page posts it (VerifyEmail.tsx:87).

claims.claim: If it is not there either, request a new verification email from the dashboard.
claims.evidence: The resend button exists on the registration page (Register.tsx:128) and on the verification page (VerifyEmail.tsx:87); no file under web/src/app offers it, so the customer does not find it in the dashboard.

claims.claim: A new verification email arrives. The answer is the same whether or not the address exists, so nobody can learn yours from the response.
claims.evidence: resend-verification always answers 200 with the same message and only sends when the address exists and is unverified (auth.ts:425-433).

claims.claim: Sign in with your email address and password. The session is stored in an HttpOnly cookie, so it survives a page reload but is not readable by scripts in the browser.
claims.evidence: The session cookie is set with httpOnly true and sameSite lax (auth.ts:254-262) and the session persists across requests (api/tests/auth.test.ts:100), but no test asserts the HttpOnly attribute itself.

claims.claim: Every request that changes something also needs the X-CSRF-Token header, whose value is the readable bm_csrf cookie.
claims.evidence: The CSRF plugin reads the x-csrf-token header and compares it with the bm_csrf cookie (csrf.ts:34, auth.ts:13); api/tests/auth.test.ts:139-156 refuses a state change without the header and accepts it with the header.

claims.claim: Forgotten password? Use the reset link on the sign-in page. Blipmade emails a link that opens the settings page with a token, and you set the new password there.
claims.evidence: The reset link points at /reset-password?token=... (email-templates.ts:61) and that page reads the token from the query (ResetPassword.tsx:51); it is not the settings page.

claims.claim: Still blocked? Open a ticket and describe what you see. The support queue is in your dashboard.
claims.evidence: POST /tickets creates a ticket of the signed-in account (tickets.ts:169-207) and the dashboard carries the ticket list (web/src/nav.ts:18 lists Support).

claims.claim: The catalog lists every app and database with its minimum resources and starting price.
claims.evidence: GET /catalog/products returns the visible and priced products with minRam, minDisk and the price (catalog.ts:96-130, 165-176); api/tests/catalog.test.ts:79 covers the public catalog.

claims.claim: Open an app to see its page in this documentation, including the first-run steps.
claims.evidence: Neither ProductPage.tsx nor DeployCatalog.tsx contains a link to the documentation; the docs live at /docs (routes.tsx:110) and the app page is not reachable from the catalog.

claims.claim: The configurator opens with the minimum configuration selected.
claims.evidence: The catalog carries defaultRam, defaultCpu and defaultDisk (catalog.ts:106-108) that the seeded products define (seed.ts:66-68).

claims.claim: Set the memory, the CPU and the disk for the instance. The price is calculated on the server for exactly the configuration you pick, so the number you see is the number you pay.
claims.evidence: priceConfiguration prices the exact configuration (pricing.ts:65-79) and the quote is built on the server (orders.ts:109); api/tests/catalog-pricing.test.ts and api/tests/order-amounts.test.ts cover the amounts.

claims.claim: You can add resources later from the instance page, and the price difference is shown before you confirm.
claims.evidence: GET /instances/:id/resources/quote returns currentPrice, newPrice and priceDelta (upgrades.ts:204-211); api/tests/upgrades.test.ts:103 quotes a change without touching the instance. The quote itself touches no panel.

claims.claim: Confirm the quote and place the order.
claims.evidence: POST /orders writes the order with its number and total (orders.ts:125-183) and the billing page lists the invoices (Billing.tsx:572-575).

claims.claim: The order appears in your billing history with its number and total.
claims.evidence: The order carries number, total, discount and currency (orders.ts:125-133) and the invoice list is rendered on the billing page (Billing.tsx:572-575).

claims.claim: You are sent to the payment page to finish the payment.
claims.evidence: The checkout exists (api/src/routes/orders.ts:249) but PAYMENTS_ENABLED=false in .env and api/src/env.ts:152 defaults it to false, so paymentState() answers 'Payments are not available at the moment: payments are turned off on this environment' (api/src/services/stripe.ts:110-116) and no session is created. The Stripe key in .env is a test key (sk_test), so even with payments on, no real money is taken. The documentation must not imply a real payment.

claims.claim: The order is marked as paid and provisioning starts.
claims.evidence: The webhook marks the order paid and the provisioning starts (api/src/routes/orders.ts:318, api/src/services/provisioning.ts:159), but the webhook that carries the money never arrives while payments are off, so the instance is never provisioned from a paid order today.

claims.claim: The status moves from pending to provisioning and finally to online.
claims.evidence: The provisioning moves the instance to PROVISIONING (provisioning.ts:159) and to ONLINE with the order FULFILLED (provisioning.ts:1645-1666).

claims.claim: The instance appears in your dashboard with its address.
claims.evidence: GET /instances lists the instances of the account (instances.ts:113) and GET /instances/:id/allocations gives the ip and port (instance-server.ts:713-735).

claims.claim: Open the address of the instance and complete the setup of the app itself: the installer, the first account or the import of your data. Every app has its own first-run steps in this documentation.
claims.evidence: The platform installs no application: it writes a small Node.js HTTP server (package.json, index.js, README.md) into the container (starter-apps.ts:84-160, provisioning.ts:301-345), which api/tests/starter-app.test.ts:36 checks. There is no WordPress, Ghost or Forgejo installer to complete.

claims.claim: The instance shows degraded: check the metrics page, the instance is running but short of resources.
claims.evidence: GET /instances/:id/metrics exists (instances.ts:191) but no file under web/src calls it, so the customer has no metrics page; DEGRADED is never written by the code (only PENDING, PROVISIONING, ONLINE, RESTARTING, STOPPED, FAILED, SUSPENDED, CANCELLED are).

claims.claim: The instance failed: open a ticket with the instance attached so support sees the right context.
claims.evidence: A ticket accepts an instanceId and the route checks that the instance belongs to the account (tickets.ts:180, 186-189).

claims.claim: Memory (RAM) - how much an application may use at once. It is the first limit most applications hit.
claims.evidence: The memory of an instance is the memory limit of the container build (application.ts:147-197) and the catalog refuses a value outside the minimum and maximum (pricing.ts:150).

claims.claim: CPU - how much processing time the instance gets.
claims.evidence: The catalog publishes minCpu and maxCpu (catalog.ts:102, 105) and the price of the extra CPU is calculated on the server (pricing.ts:151, 75).

claims.claim: Disk - how much data the instance can keep. Growing the disk keeps the data that is already there.
claims.evidence: A resize updates the build limits of the same server (application.ts:147-197) and the files of the container are not touched, so the data stays.

claims.claim: Blipmade never calculates prices in the browser. The server takes your configuration and returns the subtotal, any discount and the total. What you see in the dashboard is what you are charged.
claims.evidence: The quote is built on the server and carries total, discount and per-line totals (orders.ts:109-133); api/tests/order-amounts.test.ts covers the amounts and api/tests/catalog-pricing.test.ts the price book.

claims.claim: Prices are monthly and in euros. There are no setup fees.
claims.evidence: The seeded prices are period MONTHLY in currency EUR (seed.ts:212) and the catalog returns that period and currency (catalog.ts:130); neither ProductPrice nor Order has a setup-fee field in api/prisma/schema.prisma.

claims.claim: Go to the instance page and find the resources section.
claims.evidence: The instance page carries a Resources tab (InstanceDetail.tsx:100) that reads the quote route (instances.ts:283).

claims.claim: The server applies the change and returns the new price together with the difference to your current price.
claims.evidence: PUT /instances/:id/resources quotes the change with currentPrice, newPrice and priceDelta (instances.ts:305-355, upgrades.ts:204-211).

claims.claim: The instance keeps running on the new resources and the difference is added to your next invoice.
claims.evidence: A change that costs more is not applied at once: the quote sets requiresPayment (upgrades.ts:210), the route creates an UPGRADE order and returns a checkout (instances.ts:322-345) and the change is applied only after the payment is confirmed (api/tests/upgrades.test.ts:122, 148). Only a change that costs less is applied at once and credited on the next invoice (upgrades.ts:415, billing.ts:212-215).

claims.claim: Disk cannot shrink below the data that is already there. If you lower the disk size below what your files occupy, the change is refused.
claims.evidence: validateConfiguration only compares the new values with the minimum and the maximum of the product (pricing.ts:141-153); nothing compares the new disk with the files that are on the instance.

claims.claim: Watch the metrics page for a day before you resize. It shows the real memory and CPU use, which is a better guide than a guess.
claims.evidence: GET /instances/:id/metrics exists (instances.ts:191) but no file under web/src calls it and the instance tabs are Overview, Console, Files, Databases, Backups, Network, Startup, Schedules, Settings, Activity, Resources, Domains (InstanceDetail.tsx:89-102). There is no metrics page.

claims.claim: The billing page shows your monthly estimate, the end of the current period, the payment method on file and every invoice we issued.
claims.evidence: The page renders the estimate, the period end, the payment method (Billing.tsx:430-446) and the invoice panel (Billing.tsx:572-575) from GET /billing/summary and GET /billing/invoices (billing.ts:46, 264).

claims.claim: The monthly estimate is the sum of what your instances cost at their current resources. It is an estimate, because the final invoice is calculated when the period closes.
claims.evidence: The summary is computed from the current subscriptions of the account and the page labels it as an estimate (billing.ts:200-230, Billing.tsx:430-432).

claims.claim: The period end tells you when the current period closes and when a cancellation would take effect.
claims.evidence: The page shows the current period end (Billing.tsx:435) and the cancel action sets cancelAtPeriodEnd (billing.ts:329-360, api/src/routes/instances.ts:407).

claims.claim: The payment method shows which card is charged. Change it in the payment provider, not here.
claims.evidence: POST /billing/payment-method opens a session of the payment provider (billing.ts:389-396) and the page links to it (Billing.tsx:455-468).

claims.claim: Every invoice has a number, an amount, a tax amount and a total.
claims.evidence: GET /billing/invoices returns the invoices of the account (billing.ts:264-307) and the Invoice model carries number, subtotal, tax and total in api/prisma/schema.prisma.

claims.claim: Each invoice can be opened in the browser or downloaded as a PDF.
claims.evidence: Each invoice row links to hostedUrl and offers the PDF at pdfUrl (Billing.tsx:630-690).

claims.claim: The payment provider opens in a secure page to collect the new card.
claims.evidence: createBillingPortal creates a billing portal session (api/src/services/stripe.ts:922-936) but throws payments_unavailable while PAYMENTS_ENABLED=false (stripe.ts:923-925, api/src/env.ts:152), which is the value in .env; the Stripe key in .env is a test key (sk_test), so even with payments on no real card would be charged. The customer cannot open a portal today.

claims.claim: Blipmade never sees or stores your card details. That happens entirely in the payment provider.
claims.evidence: The card is collected in a session of the provider (stripe.ts:931-934) and the platform only stores the customer id.

claims.claim: A failed payment puts the subscription in a past due state and the instance is stopped after a grace period. Update the payment method and the instance is started again.
claims.evidence: The subscription becomes PAST_DUE (billing.ts:836), the grace lasts 7 days (billing.ts:49) and after it the instance is stopped and marked SUSPENDED (billing.ts:1548-1560); the customer starts it again with the power route (api/src/routes/instances.ts:148-188). The sentence does not say how long the grace is or that the data is kept.

claims.claim: A resize changes the resources of the running instance. Your files, your database and your configuration stay where they are, and the instance keeps its address.
claims.evidence: The resize changes the build limits of the same server (upgrades.ts:240, application.ts:147-197) and the allocation is not replaced, so the address stays (instance-server.ts:713-735).

claims.claim: Resizing is not a reinstall. Nothing is reinstalled, so nothing has to be migrated.
claims.evidence: The reinstall is a separate route that wipes the container (instance-server.ts:1163-1200); the resize route never touches the files.

claims.claim: The server returns the new price and the difference to your current price.
claims.evidence: quoteResourceChange returns currentPrice, newPrice and priceDelta (upgrades.ts:204-211); api/tests/upgrades.test.ts:103 covers it.

claims.claim: The difference is added to the next invoice.
claims.evidence: An increase has to be paid before it is applied: the quote sets requiresPayment (upgrades.ts:210), the route creates an UPGRADE order with a checkout (instances.ts:322-345) and the change is applied only after the payment is confirmed (api/tests/upgrades.test.ts:122, 148). Only a decrease is credited on the next invoice (upgrades.ts:415, billing.ts:212-215).

claims.claim: Disk cannot shrink below the space your files already use, and memory below what the application needs to start.
claims.evidence: Only the minimum and the maximum of the product are checked (pricing.ts:141-153); the size of the data is never compared with the new size.

claims.claim: Stop the instance before a large downgrade. It releases memory and makes the change predictable.
claims.evidence: The customer can stop the instance at any time (instances.ts:148-188) and a resize neither stops nor starts the container (upgrades.ts:240), so the advice holds.

claims.claim: Cancelling an instance ends the subscription at the end of the period you already paid for. The instance keeps running and keeps its address until then.
claims.evidence: The cancel route sets cancelAtPeriodEnd and leaves the instance running (instances.ts:405-408) and api/tests/billing.test.ts:86 withdraws a service whose paid period ended after a cancellation; only the call that stops the container is replaced in that suite.

claims.claim: Nothing is deleted before the period ends, so you can resume the subscription from the billing page if you change your mind.
claims.evidence: POST /billing/subscriptions/:id/resume clears cancelAtPeriodEnd (billing.ts:361-388, billing.ts:1398) and the billing page offers it.

claims.claim: Find the cancel action on the instance page.
claims.evidence: The instance page carries a Cancel instance panel that posts /instances/:id/cancel (InstanceDetail.tsx:526-540, 568-592).

claims.claim: The instance is stopped and the data is removed from the node. Download anything you still need before the period ends - the file browser is the last place to get it.
claims.evidence: At the end of the period the instance is stopped and the data is exported (billing.ts:716-733), but the service is kept for the retention term of 30 days by default (billing.ts:78, 592) and the deletion runs only when the operator has switched the auto-delete on, which is off by default (billing.ts:447). The data is not removed at the end of the period.

claims.claim: After the period ends the data is gone. Take your own backup before you let the subscription run out.
claims.evidence: The service is kept for the retention term, the data of the customer is exported before anything is deleted (billing.ts:573-631) and the customer is told the date (billing.ts:609-615). The data is not gone at the end of the period.

claims.claim: Cancelling an instance ends the subscription at the end of the period you already paid for.
claims.evidence: No money is given back for a cancellation: the route only sets cancelAtPeriodEnd (api/src/routes/instances.ts:405-408) and the period that was paid is not prorated (api/src/services/billing.ts:1521-1524). The only automatic refunds are a failed provisioning and a refused paid plan change (web/src/legal/documents/refund.tsx:65-86); there is no customer-facing refund route. The page says nothing about refunds, so the rebuild must.

pages.title: Attach a domain to an instance

claims.claim: Go to the instance page and add a domain.
claims.evidence: POST /instances/:id/domains claims a hostname for an instance of the account (domains.ts:271-386) and the instance page carries a Domains tab (InstanceDetail.tsx:101).

claims.claim: The domain appears with the DNS records you have to create.
claims.evidence: The serialized domain carries dnsRecords with name, type and value (domains.ts:223-253), built by dnsRecordsFor (gateway.ts:406-411).

claims.claim: The domain shows a name, a type and a value for every record it needs.
claims.evidence: The A record, the CNAME of www and the TXT of the proof are all returned with a name, a type and a value (domains.ts:225-228, gateway.ts:406-411).

claims.claim: Create the records the instance listed at your DNS provider. The values come from the instance, so copy them exactly as shown.
claims.evidence: The records are computed from the hostname and the target of the platform (domains.ts:224-228, gateway.ts:406-411); the platform never writes the DNS of the customer.

claims.claim: Add the TXT record the domain shows: the name and the value are on the domain itself. An address record is not enough, because every customer points at the same address.
claims.evidence: Every claim gets a random token of 24 characters (domains.ts:295) and only a TXT record with that token counts (domains.ts:415-416, dns.ts:91); api/tests/domains.test.ts:279 covers the rule but replaces the resolver and the gateway, so the DNS read itself is not proven.

claims.claim: Start the verification. Blipmade reads the TXT record and compares it with the token of the domain.
claims.evidence: POST /domains/:id/verify resolves the TXT record and compares it with the token (domains.ts:415-416, dns.ts:60-91); api/tests/domains.test.ts:298 activates a hostname when the token matches, but the resolver is replaced in that suite.

claims.claim: The status moves from verifying to active.
claims.evidence: A hostname whose proof was accepted is routed and becomes ACTIVE (domains.ts:441-456) and the answer lower-cases the state (domains.ts:218-221); api/tests/domains.test.ts:298 covers it with the gateway replaced.

claims.claim: The status stays verifying: The TXT record is not visible yet or does not carry the expected value. Wait for the DNS to spread and verify again.
claims.evidence: A claim that is never proven expires after seven days and the hostname becomes free again (domains.ts:45-46, 195-204, 406-408); api/tests/domains.test.ts:226 'lets an expired claim go'. The answer does not say that the claim runs out.

claims.claim: The status turns to error: The domain shows the last error it hit.
claims.evidence: A gateway validation error sets the state ERROR and writes lastError (domains.ts:463-465), and the serialized domain carries lastError (domains.ts:237).

claims.claim: The hostname resolves but the site is empty: The instance is stopped or is not listening on the port of the domain. Check the status and the target port of the domain.
claims.evidence: The domain exposes status and targetPort (domains.ts:234-235) and the gateway only serves the states ONLINE, RESTARTING and DEGRADED (domain-routing.ts:24).

claims.claim: The hostname is proven to be yours.
claims.evidence: The documentation never says what happens to a hostname that is not proven: the gateway refuses to route a hostname without a verifiedAt (api/src/services/gateway.ts:310-312) and a claim that is never proven expires after seven days, after which the hostname is free again (api/src/routes/domains.ts:45-46, 195-204, 406-408); api/tests/domains.test.ts:430 and 226 cover both rules.

claims.claim: Every domain in your dashboard lists the records it expects, each with a name, a type and a value. Blipmade does not guess them: it tells you what to create at your DNS provider.
claims.evidence: The records are computed from the hostname and returned with name, type and value (domains.ts:223-228, gateway.ts:406-411); the platform never writes the DNS of the customer (web/src/app/EmailHosting.tsx:390 says the same for mail).

claims.claim: A record for the bare hostname, usually an A record with an address.
claims.evidence: dnsRecordsFor returns an A record for the hostname that points at the gateway address (gateway.ts:406-409).

claims.claim: A CNAME record for the subdomains you want, pointing at the bare hostname.
claims.evidence: The platform asks for one CNAME: www.<hostname> pointing at the bare hostname (gateway.ts:409). It never asks for a CNAME per subdomain, and a subdomain other than www is not routed until it is claimed and proven on its own.

claims.claim: A TXT record that proves the hostname belongs to you. The domain shows the name and the value.
claims.evidence: The TXT record with the token is part of the answer (domains.ts:226-228) and the name it must be published under is computed by verificationHostFor (dns.ts:34); api/tests/domains.test.ts:162 covers the token and the name with the resolver replaced.

claims.claim: Nothing else. Do not add a second A record for the same name, because the resolver has to pick one.
claims.evidence: The platform asks for exactly three records: A, CNAME of www and TXT of the proof (gateway.ts:406-411, domains.ts:225-228).

claims.claim: If your provider has a CNAME flattening or proxy setting, turn it off for these records. A proxied hostname does not answer the verification check.
claims.evidence: The proof is read from the resolver (dns.ts:60-91), and a proxied name does not publish the TXT record, so the check cannot succeed.

claims.claim: Propagation is the time between creating a record and every resolver seeing it. It is usually minutes and at worst a few hours, and it depends on the TTL of the record rather than on Blipmade.
claims.evidence: The platform reads the TXT record through the resolver and does not control the TTL of the record (dns.ts:60-91); the claim expires after seven days (api/src/routes/domains.ts:46).

claims.claim: Automatic certificate issuance for attached hostnames is Planned. Blipmade does not hand out certificates yet, and it does not ask you to upload one either.
claims.evidence: The route the platform writes into Caddy is a plain reverse_proxy with no TLS policy (gateway.ts:254-265) and there is no ACME or Let's Encrypt client in api/src; the edge Caddyfile only covers the platform's own domain (deploy/edge/Caddyfile:55-90).

claims.claim: Until certificates are issued automatically, use HTTPS with a certificate you control - for example from your own DNS provider - or keep the instance behind the hostname you already secured.
claims.evidence: The customer route is a plain reverse_proxy and the platform terminates no TLS for customer hostnames (gateway.ts:254-265, 309-322), so a certificate at the customer's own provider does not protect the hostname the platform routes; the platform-managed hostname has no HTTPS at all.

claims.claim: This page is updated when the status endpoint of a domain reports a certificate.
claims.evidence: The domain answer carries no certificate and no TLS state (domains.ts:223-253) and there is no certificate in the domain model of api/prisma/schema.prisma:820-841; the only certificate the platform watches is the one of the mail server (ops-health.ts:675-690).

claims.claim: Go to the files section of the instance.
claims.evidence: The instance page carries a Files tab (InstanceDetail.tsx:92) that reads GET /instances/:id/files (instance-server.ts:163-186).

claims.claim: Open folders to see what is inside, and go back with the breadcrumb.
claims.evidence: The files route lists a directory of the container (instance-server.ts:163-186) and the tab walks it with a breadcrumb (web/src/app/instance/FilesTab.tsx).

claims.claim: Open a text file to see its content.
claims.evidence: GET /instances/:id/file reads a file of the container (instance-server.ts:188-198).

claims.claim: Edit the content and save the file.
claims.evidence: PUT /instances/:id/file writes the whole file back (instance-server.ts:200-219).

claims.claim: Saving replaces the whole file. If the application is running and holds that file open, it may keep running with the old content until it is restarted.
claims.evidence: The route writes the body as the whole file (instance-server.ts:200-219) and nothing signals the process that runs inside the container.

claims.claim: Delete the file and confirm.
claims.evidence: DELETE /instances/:id/file removes the file of the container (instance-server.ts:220-246).

claims.claim: A deleted file cannot be recovered from the dashboard. There is no trash folder and no automatic backup yet.
claims.evidence: There is no trash folder, but the platform has a customer backup that archives the files of the container and is not mentioned anywhere in the documentation (instance-server.ts:612-641, web/src/app/instance/BackupsTab.tsx:25, 175). The sentence reads as if no copy of the files can exist.

claims.claim: The file browser is meant for configuration and small edits. For large uploads, use the console: a download in the instance is faster and does not depend on the browser.
claims.evidence: The upload route is bounded (instance-server.ts:304-354) and the customer can run a command in the container (instances.ts:253-282).

claims.claim: Go to the console section of the instance.
claims.evidence: The instance page carries a Console tab (InstanceDetail.tsx:91) and GET /instances/:id/console plus the websocket /console/stream exist (instances.ts:221-252).

claims.claim: The console connects and shows the output of the application.
claims.evidence: The websocket forwards the browser to the console of the panel with the key of the customer added by the server (instances.ts:248-252).

claims.claim: The console attaches to the process of the instance as the user the application runs as.
claims.evidence: The console is the console of the server of the panel, reached with the key of the customer (instances.ts:221-252); api/tests/instance-operations.test.ts:306 'never shows the key of the panel or the address of the console'.

claims.claim: It does not give you the privileges of the platform. You cannot manage other instances or the billing from inside the console.
claims.evidence: The console is a console of one container of the customer and the key of the panel never leaves the server (api/src/routes/instances.ts:430-434, instance-operations.test.ts:306-322).

claims.claim: It does not survive a rebuild of the instance. Anything you installed outside your project is gone after the next rebuild.
claims.evidence: The reinstall route says that everything the customer stored in the container is lost and erases the files (instance-server.ts:1163-1200, reinstall.ts:127).

claims.claim: It does not replace a backup. Keep your own copy of what matters.
claims.evidence: The backup of the panel archives the files of the container (instance-server.ts:612-641); the advice to keep a copy of what matters is right for anything that is not a file of the container.

claims.claim: Put anything you want to run on every start into the startup command of the instance. The console is for the one-off job.
claims.evidence: The customer reads and changes the startup command of the server at GET and PUT /instances/:id/startup (instance-server.ts:840-921).

claims.claim: Signing in creates a session on the server and hands the browser an HttpOnly cookie. Scripts in the page cannot read it, and it is renewed as long as you keep working.
claims.evidence: The cookie is HttpOnly (auth.ts:254-262) but the term is a fixed 14 days from the sign-in (SESSION_TTL_MS, auth.ts:14, 238-242); only lastSeenAt is touched by the activity (auth.ts:311-313), the term itself is never extended.

claims.claim: A list of the devices signed in to your account is not available yet. Until it is, signing out of a shared computer is the safest move.
claims.evidence: GET /settings/sessions lists the sessions of the account and DELETE /settings/sessions/:id closes one of them (settings.ts:490-557), the panel shows the list (Settings.tsx:157, 428-441) and api/tests/settings.test.ts:173 'lists the devices and closes one of them'.

claims.claim: The link in the email carries a token that verifies the address.
claims.evidence: The verification token is stored hashed and consumed once (auth.ts:394-406).

claims.claim: Request a new verification email from the dashboard.
claims.evidence: The resend button is on the registration page (Register.tsx:128) and on the verification page (VerifyEmail.tsx:87); no file under web/src/app offers it, so it is not in the dashboard.

claims.claim: There is no password change endpoint for a signed-in account, so the password is changed with a reset token instead.
claims.evidence: POST /settings/password changes the password of a signed-in account, asks for the current one and closes the other sessions (settings.ts:434-489), the panel offers it (Settings.tsx:156, 340-420) and api/tests/settings.test.ts:127-172 covers it.

claims.claim: Open the settings page and choose Request a password reset link.
claims.evidence: The reset is asked for on the /forgot-password page, which is linked from the sign-in page (Login.tsx:121, ForgotPassword.tsx:55); there is no such control in web/src/app/Settings.tsx.

claims.claim: Blipmade emails a link to the address on the account.
claims.evidence: forgot-password sends the reset mail when the address exists (auth.ts:437-451) and the answer is the same for every address (auth.ts:452-457).

claims.claim: The link opens the settings page with a token.
claims.evidence: The link points at /reset-password?token=... (email-templates.ts:61) and that page reads the token from the query (ResetPassword.tsx:51); it is not the settings page.

claims.claim: Enter the new password twice and confirm.
claims.evidence: The page posts the token and the new password twice before it sends it (ResetPassword.tsx:78) and the route hashes it (auth.ts:461-479).

claims.claim: You are signed out of the old session and the new password works from now on.
claims.evidence: The reset deletes every session of the account in the same transaction as the new hash (auth.ts:474-479); no test asserts the deletion of the sessions of a reset.

claims.claim: Signing out ends the session on the server and clears the cookie in the browser. The settings page has a button for it.
claims.evidence: POST /auth/logout deletes the session and clears the cookie (auth.ts:364-392, auth.ts:267-273) and the settings page offers it.

claims.claim: Go to the startup and environment section of the instance.
claims.evidence: The instance page carries a Startup tab (InstanceDetail.tsx:96) that reads GET /instances/:id/startup (instance-server.ts:840-856).

claims.claim: You see the current variables and the startup command.
claims.evidence: The route answers the image, the startup command and the whole environment of the server (instance-server.ts:851-855).

claims.claim: Add or change the variables the application needs and save.
claims.evidence: PUT and PATCH /instances/:id/startup merge the new values into the environment of the server (instance-server.ts:864-921).

claims.claim: The instance restarts with the new environment.
claims.evidence: The route writes the environment into the server of the panel and returns; no start, stop or restart is triggered (instance-server.ts:864-910, application.ts:208-231). The new values apply the next time the instance starts.

claims.claim: Environment variables are readable by anyone who can open the instance and by everything that runs inside it. Keep tokens and database passwords out of your repository.
claims.evidence: The route returns the environment of the server in plain text to the owner of the instance (instance-server.ts:847-855) and the container reads it as its own environment.

claims.claim: The startup command is what the instance runs when it starts. Put your migrations and your installs in it, so a restart comes back in a working state.
claims.evidence: The startup command is the container start-up command of the panel and the customer can change it (instance-server.ts:851-853, application.ts:208-231).

claims.claim: The API lives under /api of the same address you use for the dashboard. Requests are same-origin and carry your session cookie. Every request that changes something also needs the X-CSRF-Token header, whose value is the readable bm_csrf cookie.
claims.evidence: The API is mounted under the prefix /api (app.ts:223) and the CSRF plugin checks the header against the bm_csrf cookie (csrf.ts:34, auth.ts:13); api/tests/phase2-session-security.test.ts covers it.

claims.claim: Programmatic keys are Planned. The API does not expose key management, so the dashboard does not offer a button to create one.
claims.evidence: There is no API key model in api/prisma/schema.prisma and no key route in api/src/routes; the only credentials are the panel key per customer (api/src/services/panel/operations.ts).

claims.claim: Until then, scripts use the session of an account, which means they need the cookie and the CSRF token of a signed-in user.
claims.evidence: A request is identified by the session cookie (auth.ts:155-158) and a writing request needs the CSRF token (csrf.ts:34).

claims.claim: Do not put the session cookie of a real account into a script that runs unattended. Treat every cookie like a password.
claims.evidence: A session can be closed by the customer at any time (settings.ts:533-557) and the account keeps at most 20 sessions (auth.ts:132), so a script that holds a cookie is breakable from the account.

claims.claim: The instance page shows the state of the instance.
claims.evidence: The instance page renders the state in a pill (InstanceDetail.tsx:673) and GET /instances/:id returns it (instances.ts:128-147).

claims.claim: You see whether it is online, starting, stopped or degraded.
claims.evidence: The states the code writes are PENDING, PROVISIONING, ONLINE, RESTARTING, STOPPED, FAILED, SUSPENDED and CANCELLED (schema.prisma:737-747, instances.ts:173, provisioning.ts:159, 217, 1645); there is no 'starting' state and DEGRADED is never written.

claims.claim: Use the start action on the instance.
claims.evidence: POST /instances/:id/power starts, stops and restarts the server of the panel (instances.ts:148-189).

claims.claim: The metrics page shows the memory, the CPU and the network of the instance.
claims.evidence: GET /instances/:id/metrics returns the usage (instances.ts:191-220) but no file under web/src calls it and there is no metrics page in the tabs (InstanceDetail.tsx:89-102).

claims.claim: An instance that runs out of memory is stopped or degraded, and the metric explains why.
claims.evidence: There is no metric in the interface (see above) and the platform never writes DEGRADED; the only note about a container that is alive without a health check is the one of the operator (runtime-state.ts:200-250).

claims.claim: The events of an instance record what happened to it: when it was started, stopped, resized or renamed.
claims.evidence: GET /instances/:id/events returns the events (instances.ts:356-374) and the rename and power routes write events (instances.ts:175, 375-391); the Activity tab shows them (web/src/app/instance/ActivityTab.tsx:16).

claims.claim: The console shows the output of the application, including the reason it did not start.
claims.evidence: The console stream is the output of the container of the panel (instances.ts:221-252).

claims.claim: If the instance stopped on its own and the payment method is old, the subscription may be past due. The billing page shows the state of every subscription and lets you update the card.
claims.evidence: An unpaid invoice puts the subscription in PAST_DUE (billing.ts:836) and the instance is suspended after the grace (billing.ts:1548-1560); the billing page lists the subscriptions (Billing.tsx:520-560) and the payment method panel (Billing.tsx:455-468).

claims.claim: Still stuck? Open a ticket and attach the instance. Include what you expected, what happened, and the relevant part of the console output.
claims.evidence: A ticket takes an instanceId that must belong to the account (tickets.ts:180, 186-189) and attachments of a bounded size (tickets.ts:61-71).

claims.claim: Every product in the catalog has a minimum and a maximum for memory, CPU and disk. The configurator refuses anything outside those values, so an instance can never ask for more than the plan allows.
claims.evidence: The catalog publishes min and max for ram, cpu and disk (catalog.ts:102-111) and validateConfiguration refuses anything outside them (pricing.ts:141-153); api/tests/upgrades.test.ts:227 'refuses a change outside the limits of the product'.

claims.claim: Those bounds come from the catalog itself. You do not have to remember them: the form shows what is allowed.
claims.evidence: The bounds are the fields of the catalog answer (catalog.ts:102-111) and the deploy form reads them.

claims.claim: Blipmade does not publish quotas for traffic, tickets, accounts or the number of instances you may run.
claims.evidence: There is no traffic quota, no ticket quota and no cap of instances per account; the only count on instances is the fulfilment check of an order (billing.ts:1652-1655).

claims.claim: Nothing here is a hidden limit you can trip over: if a limit exists, it is shown where you would hit it.
claims.evidence: There are limits that the interface never shows: 20 sessions per account (auth.ts:132), 100 environment variables per instance (bounded.ts:19) and a rate limit on every writing route, for example 30 writes a minute on an account and 10 mails a quarter of an hour (rate-limit.ts:72-85).

claims.claim: Traffic and bandwidth ceilings per instance: not available yet.
claims.evidence: The usage the platform reports is the usage of the node, not a ceiling it enforces (instances.ts:191-220); no traffic quota exists in api/src.

claims.claim: A maximum number of instances per account: not available yet.
claims.evidence: The list of the instances has no cap and the provisioning does not count the instances of an account (instances.ts:113-127).

claims.claim: Published response times for support tickets: not available yet.
claims.evidence: A ticket has no promised answer and the platform's own service level page says that there is no response time and no service credit (sla.tsx:41-46). The platform publishes no availability figure either: the service level page states that it does not guarantee that the service will be reachable at any given moment (sla.tsx:41-46) and the status page says that the 90-day uptime history is not available yet (Status.tsx:242). The documentation makes no uptime promise today, so there is none to remove - the rebuild must not add one.

claims.claim: Give an application the memory it needs. Applications that are short of memory are the most common cause of a degraded instance.
claims.evidence: The memory of an instance is the memory limit of the container (application.ts:147-197) and the platform never marks an instance as degraded, so the sentence names a state that does not exist.

claims.claim: Watch the disk. Databases, logs and uploads all end up on the same disk, and a full disk stops the application.
claims.evidence: The instance has one disk allocation and one disk limit (instance-server.ts:713-735, application.ts:147-197).

claims.claim: Do not use an instance to send bulk mail or to run something that has nothing to do with the application you deployed.
claims.evidence: The acceptable use document of the platform carries the same rule; the documentation must point at it.

claims.claim: Blipmade does not take automatic backups of your data yet.
claims.evidence: The first half is true: there is no scheduled backup. But the platform has a customer backup that the documentation never mentions, and the two systems must not be confused with each other. The customer backup is manual: POST /instances/:id/backups asks the panel to write an archive of the FILES OF THE CONTAINER on the node (instance-server.ts:612-641, panel/operations.ts:226-244); it can be downloaded as a .tar.gz and restoring it REPLACES the files of the container (instance-server.ts:643-683); the number of backups is the limit of the egg of the panel and the platform keeps no time limit of its own (pterodactyl/types.ts:34, 109); the panel already shows it (web/src/app/instance/BackupsTab.tsx:25, 141-176). The platform backup (scripts/backup.sh:1-40, 62-96) is a different thing: it holds the platform's own database, its configuration and the uploads, kept BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS days, and says nothing about a customer.

pages.title: The app and database page template

claims.claim: Minimum resources: {memLabel(product.minRam)} RAM - {product.minDisk} GB disk
claims.evidence: The template takes the minimum from the catalog answer (Docs.tsx:87-89, catalog.ts:103-105) so the numbers are the ones the catalog enforces (pricing.ts:141-153); the label turns MB into GB (web/src/lib/pricing.ts:213).

claims.claim: CPU: Selectable when you deploy
claims.evidence: The catalog publishes minCpu and maxCpu and the deploy form picks a value inside them (catalog.ts:102, 105).

claims.claim: Price from: {the catalog price}
claims.evidence: The template shows the price of the catalog answer (Docs.tsx:81-84) and the catalog returns the price of the price row that also prices the order (catalog.ts:70, 130).

claims.claim: Billing: Monthly, billed in euros
claims.evidence: The seeded price rows are period MONTHLY in currency EUR (seed.ts:212) and the catalog returns that period and currency (catalog.ts:130).

claims.claim: The price shown is the catalog starting price for the smallest configuration. Blipmade calculates the exact price for your configuration on the server when you deploy.
claims.evidence: priceConfiguration prices the exact configuration (pricing.ts:65-79) and the quote comes from the server (orders.ts:109); api/tests/catalog-pricing.test.ts covers the price book.

claims.claim: Environment variables are visible to everyone who can open the instance. Keep tokens and passwords out of public repositories.
claims.evidence: The environment is returned in plain text to the owner of the instance (instance-server.ts:847-855) and every process of the container reads it.

claims.claim: This app needs no environment variables for a standard install, so you can leave the variable list empty.
claims.evidence: The note is only true for the applications the customer installs himself; the platform writes its own application into the container and it reads SERVER_PORT and PORT (starter-apps.ts:77-82, 101-120), so the variable list of an empty list does not describe the instance that the platform delivers.

claims.claim: Two variables matter for a normal install. The editor reads them from the instance environment.
claims.evidence: The platform sets no variable of an application: it writes three files (package.json, index.js, README.md) that read SERVER_PORT and PORT (api/src/services/starter-apps.ts:77-82, 84-120, api/src/services/provisioning.ts:301-345). The only variable a seeded product declares is MAIN_FILE for the Node.js egg (api/prisma/seed.ts:126). Every variable in the documented tables is written by the customer.

claims.claim: WordPress: 'WordPress is the site builder in the Blipmade catalog: blogs, company sites and small stores. You choose the memory, CPU and disk, and the instance runs the stack for you.' First run: 'Open the instance' -> 'The WordPress installer opens in your browser.', 'Choose the language', 'Create the administrator account', 'Set the permalink structure'. Environment: no variables. Backup: 'Blipmade does not take automatic backups of your data yet. Your content lives in the database and your uploads live in the files of the instance, so back up both.' Upgrade: 'Resize the instance whenever the site needs more room. WordPress keeps running while the change is applied'. Troubleshooting: 'The installer never appears', 'The installer stops at the database step', 'The site is slow or shows a database error'.
claims.evidence: The product is listed but not deployable: deployable is false, eggId is null, eggName is null and dockerImage is null, with the description 'It runs on a WordPress image of the panel, and that image is not installed on the platform yet, so it is listed but cannot be deployed' (seed.ts:66-88). It was marked as orderable and pointed at egg 15, the generic Node.js egg, which would have given the customer a Node.js container instead of WordPress; it was closed again on 2026-10-27. The platform writes its own Node.js server, not WordPress (starter-apps.ts:100-120). There is no installer, no wp-config.php and no mysqldump unless the customer installs WordPress himself.

claims.claim: Ghost: 'Ghost is a publishing platform for newsletters and member sites. It keeps its content in MySQL, so a Ghost deployment runs together with a MySQL database instance.' First run: 'Deploy a MySQL database', 'Point Ghost at the database', 'Open the setup screen', 'Create the owner account'. Environment: DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD, DB_NAME, url. Backup: 'Ghost keeps two things that matter: the MySQL database with your content, and the content folder with your theme and uploads. Blipmade does not schedule automatic backups yet.' Upgrade: 'Ghost versions are not updated by Blipmade.' Troubleshooting: 'Ghost shows the setup screen on every restart', 'Ghost crashes right after it starts', 'No email ever arrives from Ghost'.
claims.evidence: No product with the slug ghost exists: the catalog of the seed holds five products (seed.ts:55-178) and the catalog route only returns rows that exist in the database (catalog.ts:165-197). The page is never published because availablePages only publishes a page for a product of the catalog (web/src/pages/Docs.tsx:2243-2250), and MySQL is not sold either.

claims.claim: Forgejo: 'Forgejo is a lightweight Git forge: repositories, issues, pull requests and a package registry, running on your own instance.' First run: 'Open the instance', 'Create the administrator account', 'Set the site URL', 'Create a repository'. Environment: FORGEJO__server__ROOT_URL, FORGEJO__server__DOMAIN, FORGEJO__server__SSH_DOMAIN. Backup: 'Repositories, issues and the database all live in the Forgejo data directory inside the instance. Blipmade does not take automatic backups yet.' Upgrade: 'Forgejo versions are not managed by Blipmade.' Troubleshooting: 'The installer keeps asking for the database', 'Cloning over SSH does not work', 'Pushes become slow with many repositories'.
claims.evidence: No product with the slug forgejo exists in the seed (seed.ts:55-178) and the catalog route only lists the rows of the database (catalog.ts:165-197), so the page is never published (web/src/pages/Docs.tsx:2243-2250). The answer about SSH is right: there is no SSH in the platform, only the console and the file browser.

claims.claim: Code Server: 'Code Server is the browser version of Visual Studio Code. It runs on your instance, so your editor, your terminal and your project files are the same machine.' First run: 'Open the instance', 'Set the access password', 'Open your project folder', 'Open a terminal'. Environment: PASSWORD, PORT. Backup: 'Your projects are plain files on the instance. Blipmade does not back them up for you yet.' Upgrade: 'Code Server is stateless: it only serves the files of the instance.' Troubleshooting: 'The editor does not load', 'The terminal says command not found', 'Installed tools disappear after a restart'.
claims.evidence: The product is listed but not deployable: deployable false, eggId null, with eggName 'Code-Server' and the image ghcr.io/ptero-eggs/yolks:nodejs_18 (seed.ts:92-116). The egg is not imported in the panel yet, so the product stays closed. The container would receive the Code-Server egg and not the Node.js server of the platform, and the password of the editor is made for every instance and read in the console of the service (api/src/services/instance-credentials.ts).

claims.claim: Uptime Kuma: 'Uptime Kuma watches your endpoints over HTTP, TCP or ping and publishes a status page you can share with your own users.' First run: 'Open the instance', 'Read the credentials from the console', 'Change the password immediately', 'Add a monitor and a status page'. Environment: no variables. Backup: 'Monitors, status pages and the account live in the Uptime Kuma database in the data folder. Blipmade does not take automatic backups yet.' Upgrade: 'The Uptime Kuma version follows the image. Blipmade does not patch it in place.' Troubleshooting: 'The default password is rejected', 'Monitors report down although the target is up', 'The login page keeps loading'.
claims.evidence: The product is listed but not deployable: deployable false, eggId null, with eggName 'Uptime Kuma' and the image ghcr.io/ptero-eggs/apps:uptimekuma (seed.ts:148-170). The egg is not imported in the panel yet, so the product stays closed. The account of the administrator of Uptime Kuma is made by the application itself on the first start, and the egg carries no password.

claims.claim: Grafana: 'Grafana turns your data into dashboards. Point it at a PostgreSQL or MySQL instance, a Prometheus server, or anything else that speaks one of its data sources.' First run: 'Open the instance', 'Create the administrator account', 'Add a data source', 'Build a dashboard'. Environment: GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD, GF_USERS_ALLOW_SIGN_UP, GF_SERVER_ROOT_URL. Backup: 'Dashboards, users and the data source configuration live in the Grafana database. Blipmade does not take automatic backups yet.' Upgrade: 'The Grafana version follows the image. Blipmade does not update it in place.' Troubleshooting: 'The setup screen appears on every restart', 'The data source test fails', 'Panels are empty'.
claims.evidence: No product with the slug grafana exists in the seed (seed.ts:55-178) and the catalog route only returns the rows of the database (catalog.ts:165-197), so the page is never published (web/src/pages/Docs.tsx:2243-2250).

claims.claim: n8n: 'n8n connects services into workflows that run on a schedule or on a webhook. Workflows and credentials stay on the instance you deploy.' First run: 'Open the instance', 'Create the owner account', 'Add a credential', 'Import or build a workflow'. Environment: N8N_HOST, N8N_PORT, N8N_PROTOCOL, WEBHOOK_URL, N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY, GENERIC_TIMEZONE. Backup: 'Workflows and credentials live in the n8n database. Blipmade does not take automatic backups yet, and a backup without the encryption key is of little use.' Upgrade: 'The n8n version follows the image; Blipmade does not update it in place.' Troubleshooting: 'The owner setup screen appears on every restart', 'Webhook URLs cannot be opened', 'Credentials stopped working'.
claims.evidence: No product with the slug n8n exists in the seed (seed.ts:55-178) and the catalog route only returns the rows of the database (catalog.ts:165-197), so the page is never published (web/src/pages/Docs.tsx:2243-2250).

claims.claim: Discord Bot: 'A Discord bot is a small program that stays connected to Discord. The instance keeps it online, restarts it if it stops, and keeps its token out of your repository.' First run: 'Create the application in Discord', 'Store the token in the instance', 'Invite the bot to your server', 'Start the bot'. Environment: DISCORD_TOKEN, DISCORD_CLIENT_ID, PREFIX, NODE_ENV. Backup: 'A bot is code plus configuration. Blipmade does not back up either of them for you yet.' Upgrade: 'Small bots fit in the minimum configuration.' Troubleshooting: 'The bot never comes online', 'The bot stops after a while', 'Commands are not picked up'.
claims.evidence: This is the only product that can really be deployed (egg 15, the verified Node.js image, seed.ts:105-128) and the customer writes the bot himself, but the platform sets no restart policy for the container, so it does not restart the bot when it stops, and the backup sentence is wrong: the backup of the panel archives the files of the container, so the code is backed up (instance-server.ts:612-641, starter-apps.ts:100-120).

claims.claim: PostgreSQL: 'PostgreSQL is a relational database with a strong query planner. The instance gives you a database with its own disk, and you connect to it from anywhere the network allows.' First run: 'Deploy the database', 'Read the connection details', 'Create the database you need', 'Create an application user'. Environment: POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB, PGDATA. Backup: 'Blipmade does not schedule automatic backups for database instances yet. A dump from the console is the reliable way to keep a copy.' Upgrade: 'A major version change needs a dump and a restore into a new instance.' Troubleshooting: 'The connection is refused', 'Authentication failed', 'The database runs out of disk'.
claims.evidence: The product is listed but not deployable: deployable false, eggId null, with eggName 'Postgres 16' and the image ghcr.io/ptero-eggs/yolks:postgres_16 (seed.ts:174-198). The egg is not imported in the panel yet, so the product stays closed. The password of the superuser is made for every instance and read in the console of the service (api/src/services/instance-credentials.ts).

claims.claim: MySQL: 'MySQL is the classic relational database and the one most WordPress and Ghost setups expect. The instance runs the server, the data lives on its disk.' First run: 'Deploy MySQL', 'Read the connection details', 'Create a database and an application user', 'Check the version your client speaks'. Environment: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD, MYSQL_DATABASE, MYSQL_USER, MYSQL_PASSWORD. Backup: 'Blipmade does not schedule automatic backups for database instances yet. Dump the database from the console.' Upgrade: 'Changing the major version of MySQL is not something the dashboard can do for you.' Troubleshooting: 'Access denied for the application user', 'The server refuses to start after a password change', 'The instance runs out of disk'.
claims.evidence: No product with the slug mysql exists in the seed (seed.ts:55-178) and the catalog route only returns the rows of the database (catalog.ts:165-197), so the page is never published (web/src/pages/Docs.tsx:2243-2250). The Ghost page depends on it too.

claims.claim: Redis: 'Redis keeps data in memory, which makes it the usual choice for caches, job queues and rate limiters. It is small, fast and easy to lose, so treat it as a cache unless you have enabled persistence.' First run: 'Deploy Redis', 'Check the connection', 'Require a password', 'Decide what happens at the memory limit'. Environment: REDIS_PASSWORD, REDIS_MAXMEMORY, REDIS_MAXMEMORY_POLICY. Backup: 'Blipmade does not schedule automatic backups for database instances yet. Redis usually rebuilds its content from the application, but persistence still helps.' Upgrade: 'Resizing happens on the instance page.' Troubleshooting: 'OOM command not allowed', 'The connection drops after a while', 'The data is gone after a restart'.
claims.evidence: No product with the slug redis exists in the seed (seed.ts:55-178) and the catalog route only returns the rows of the database (catalog.ts:165-197), so the page is never published (web/src/pages/Docs.tsx:2243-2250).

claims.claim: MongoDB: 'MongoDB stores documents instead of rows, which suits data whose shape changes. The instance runs the server and keeps the data on its own disk.' First run: 'Deploy MongoDB', 'Read the connection details', 'Create the application database', 'Create an application user'. Environment: MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME, MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD, MONGO_INITDB_DATABASE. Backup: 'Blipmade does not schedule automatic backups for database instances yet. A dump from the console keeps your collections safe.' Upgrade: 'A change of the major MongoDB version is a migration, not a resize.' Troubleshooting: 'Authentication failed', 'The disk fills up', 'The connection times out'.
claims.evidence: No product with the slug mongodb exists in the seed (seed.ts:55-178) and the catalog route only returns the rows of the database (catalog.ts:165-197), so the page is never published (web/src/pages/Docs.tsx:2243-2250).

claims.claim: Blipmade does not take automatic backups of your data yet.
claims.evidence: The backup of the customer is the archive of the files of the container that the panel writes on the node at the request of the customer (api/src/routes/instance-server.ts:612-641, api/src/services/panel/operations.ts:226-244, api/tests/instance-operations.test.ts:292); it holds the files but no dump of a database that runs elsewhere and it has no schedule. The backup of the platform (scripts/backup.sh:1-40, 62-96) holds the platform's own database, its configuration and the uploads and says nothing about a customer. The two are never distinguished in the documentation.

missingJourneys: account management: name, email address and password change, closing the account, and what the closure does
dashboard navigation: where every page of the customer area lives and what it does
database connectivity and persistence: connection details, where the database of a product comes from and how the data survives a restart
custom domain ownership verification: the TXT record, the seven-day life of a claim and what happens to an unproven hostname
platform-managed domains: the address of an instance, how it is reached and when it is stable
email hosting: mailboxes, aliases, quotas, the DNS records, the webmail and the mail clients - the feature exists in the code but the mail product is not on sale
backups and recovery responsibilities: the customer backup of the panel, what it holds, where it is kept, how it is restored, and the responsibility of the customer for what it does not hold
support and support tickets: how to open a ticket, how to attach an instance and a file, and what the answer times are
notifications and preferences: the events of the account, the mail that is sent and the preferences that switch it
status, incidents and maintenance: the status page, what it reports and how a planned maintenance is announced
